issues.legal_issue: Detention for failure to pay a money decree requires more than nonpayment or the debtor’s past ability to pay; the court must find current ability coupled with refusal or neglect, or relevant past ability accompanied by bad faith, while considering pressing needs and present circumstances.
material_facts: The judgment-debtors faced execution of a money decree and a warrant for arrest and detention in civil prison.
Their immovable properties had been attached for sale and a receiver had been appointed to manage them.
The executing court had not investigated their current ability to pay or whether they had dishonestly refused or evaded payment.
The basis for the new warrant was that a similar warrant had previously been issued.
issues.conclusion: A simple failure to pay does not justify detention. Before ordering detention, the court must establish the relevant means and refusal or bad faith, and consider the debtor’s pressing needs and straitened circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 51, proviso (b), of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Order 21, rule 37, detention for a money decree is not justified by omission to pay alone. The court must find current means to pay the decree or a substantial part and refusal or neglect, or relevant past means accompanied by bad faith in liquidating the liability; it must consider pressing claims and present circumstances. The construction accords with Article 11 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the construction endorsed by the Law Commission and the cited Kerala ruling.

rule.if: money_decree_execution and (current_sufficient_means and wilful_refusal_or_neglect and no_pressing_claims or past_means and bad_faith_in_liquidating_liability)

predicates.money_decree_execution: A creditor is seeking civil detention of a debtor in execution of a money decree.
predicates.current_sufficient_means: The debtor currently has sufficient means to pay the decree or a substantial part of it.
predicates.wilful_refusal_or_neglect: The debtor has refused or neglected to pay despite having the relevant means.
predicates.no_pressing_claims: The debtor’s means are not subject to other pressing needs that materially affect the ability to pay.
predicates.past_means: The debtor previously had sufficient means to pay the decree or a substantial part of it.
predicates.bad_faith_in_liquidating_liability: The debtor acted dishonestly or in bad faith in dealing with the liability or assets relevant to its payment.

issues.definition: When a debtor is pursued for civil detention over a money decree, detention may be ordered if the debtor has current means and wilfully fails to pay without pressing claims, or previously had means and acted in bad faith in liquidating the liability.

issues.legal_issue: An international covenant does not automatically become enforceable domestic law, but it may guide interpretation of domestic law where that law is open to interpretation.
material_facts: The court considered the covenant’s prohibition on imprisonment merely for inability to fulfil a contractual obligation.
Domestic procedural law expressly provided for detention in execution of a money decree.
India was a signatory to the covenant, and Article 51(c) of the Constitution directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.
issues.conclusion: The covenant was not directly controlling as domestic law, but the domestic provision should, where interpretation permits, be read consistently with the covenant.
issues.legal_principle: International treaty obligations do not become part of domestic law without transformation into municipal law. Article 51(c) supports respect for those obligations, and where the domestic rule is doubtful it should be interpreted consistently with them. Article 11 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights therefore informs the interpretation of section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but does not itself operate as enforceable domestic law.

predicates.domestic_law_interpretation: A court is interpreting a domestic legal rule.
predicates.treaty_obligation_relevant: An international treaty obligation is relevant to the subject of the domestic rule.
predicates.treaty_not_transformed_into_domestic_law: The treaty obligation has not been made part of domestic law through legislation or another recognized transformation.

issues.definition: When a court interprets domestic law in light of a relevant treaty obligation that has not been transformed into domestic law, the treaty guides compatible interpretation but is not directly enforceable domestic law.

issues.legal_issue: Detention for inability to pay a contractual debt is incompatible with the constitutional protection of personal liberty unless the procedure establishes a wilful failure to pay despite sufficient means and accounts for pressing claims.
material_facts: The judgment-debtors faced civil detention for nonpayment of a contractual debt.
The executing court had not investigated their current ability to pay or any bad-faith refusal to pay.
Their properties had been attached and were being managed by a receiver, and the court had not considered their present financial pressures.
issues.conclusion: The provision, construed to require proof of a wilful failure to pay despite sufficient means and consideration of pressing claims, was not struck down; the court did not finally decide the validity of the provision beyond that construction.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21, read with Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution, requires a fair, just and reasonable procedure before personal liberty is taken. The principles in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration, and Sita Ram v. State of U.P. support that requirement. Imprisonment because of poverty and inability to meet a contractual liability is impermissible absent proof of a wilful failure to pay despite sufficient means and consideration of grave or pressing claims. The Court construed the proviso to section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure accordingly and did not finally adjudicate a broader challenge to its validity.

rule.if: money_decree_execution and civil_detention_sought and inability_to_pay_due_to_poverty and no_proof_of_wilful_failure_despite_means

predicates.money_decree_execution: A creditor is seeking civil detention of a debtor in execution of a money decree.
predicates.civil_detention_sought: The court is being asked to deprive the debtor of liberty by committing the debtor to civil prison.
predicates.inability_to_pay_due_to_poverty: The debtor cannot meet the contractual liability because of poverty or financial inability.
predicates.no_proof_of_wilful_failure_despite_means: There is no proof that the debtor wilfully failed to pay despite having sufficient means, with pressing claims taken into account.

issues.definition: In execution of a money decree, detention is not permissible when the debtor cannot pay because of poverty and there is no proof of wilful nonpayment despite sufficient means.

issues.legal_issue: An arrest order in execution cannot stand where the debtor’s present means and any bad-faith evasion have not been investigated and earlier findings may no longer reflect materially changed circumstances.
material_facts: The executing court issued a warrant because a similar warrant had previously been issued.
The judgment-debtors’ properties had since been attached and a receiver appointed to manage them.
The executing court had not investigated the debtors’ current ability to pay or whether they had improperly evaded payment or acted in bad faith regarding their assets.
issues.conclusion: The order under appeal was set aside and the matter remitted to the executing court for a fresh determination of the debtors’ means, present financial pressures, and any improper evasion or bad-faith conduct.
issues.legal_principle: Under the interpretation of section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the executing court must determine the debtor’s relevant means and circumstances, including pressing claims and any improper evasion or bad faith. An earlier adjudication remains binding only if relevant circumstances have not materially changed.

rule.if: money_decree_execution and detention_order_based_on_prior_process and no_current_inquiry and material_change_in_circumstances

predicates.money_decree_execution: A creditor is seeking civil detention of a debtor in execution of a money decree.
predicates.detention_order_based_on_prior_process: The court issued a detention order relying on an earlier arrest or detention process.
predicates.no_current_inquiry: The court did not investigate the debtor’s present means or relevant refusal, evasion, or bad-faith conduct.
predicates.material_change_in_circumstances: Relevant financial or property circumstances changed after the earlier assessment.

issues.definition: When a detention order in money-decree execution relies on prior process despite changed circumstances and no current inquiry, the order is set aside and the debtor’s circumstances must be assessed afresh.
